axes.question: What do you aim for?
desc: Many moves target the enemy king and pieces directly. High aggressive and tactical scores.
Many moves build lasting advantages: pawn structure, weak squares, piece placement. High positional and prophylactic scores.

axes.question: How do you treat risk?
desc: You sharpen the position and enjoy risky choices such as traps, gambles and sacrifices.
You prefer moves that hold up against any reply, and trades that tidy the position.

axes.question: Who drives the game?
desc: You take the lead, forcing your opponent's replies with threats.
You parry threats and wait for the right moment to strike back.

axes.question: How unusual are your moves?
desc: You often play moves that people at your rating rarely play, according to the human-move model Maia3.
You mostly play the natural moves people at your rating play. Not weaker, just the proven path.

AW.name: Attackers
AW.desc: Players who go for the attack and accept risk. The noisier the board, the stronger they get.

AS.name: Precision
AS.desc: Players who aim to attack without overreaching, striking sharply inside a safe frame.

PW.name: Strategists
PW.desc: Players who fight with structure and plans, and aren't afraid of complicated positions.

PS.name: Stabilizers
PS.desc: Players who collect and keep small advantages, and win by making fewer mistakes.

AWIO.tagline: Opens the attack down a road no one has taken
AWIO.summary: The Pioneer prefers new roads to well-known ones. If giving up material buys the initiative, they don't hesitate, and they drag the game into positions the opponent has never seen. When the opponent misses the right defense, the game ends fast; against accurate defense, an overreaching sacrifice can simply stay a loss.
traits: Sacrifices and surprise moves come up often
Never gives the opponent time to think
weaknesses: Material losses stick against precise defense
Plans tend to vanish once the attack is stopped
Concentration drops in quiet endgames
tips: Before a sacrifice, ask once: what is left if it gets stopped?
Practice the endgames that follow your attacks on purpose
Learning to tell a gamble from a sound sacrifice will raise your level a lot
AWIO.scene: A knight leaps over a pawn wall and targets the king

AWIE.tagline: Keeps pushing with proven attacking patterns
AWIE.summary: The Striker pulls out well-known attacking patterns at exactly the right time in sharp positions. Pawn storms, piece concentration, chains of forcing moves: they use the familiar weapons without hesitation. Once they have the initiative they rarely let go, but because the moves are standard, opponents who know the patterns can prepare for them.
traits: Checks, captures and threats come one after another
Builds familiar attacking setups again and again
Keeps pressing once the initiative is theirs
weaknesses: Easy to read for opponents who know the patterns
Forces attacks in positions that don't call for one
Switches to defense too late
tips: Prepare a second plan for positions where attacking doesn't work
Practice defensive lines for when the opponent strikes back
Learning one quiet line in your favorite opening helps a lot
AWIE.scene: Queen and rook line up on one file aiming at the king

AWRO.tagline: Turns the game around with a counterattack no one saw coming
AWRO.summary: The Hustler isn't scared when the opponent attacks first. The messier the board gets, the more chances they find, flipping the game with a counterattack nobody expected. They win a lot of lost positions, but they also create crises of their own.
traits: Answers threats with bigger threats instead of defending
Complicates the position further when worse
Never misses the moment the opponent relaxes
weaknesses: Can struggle to convert winning positions
Neglects defense while hunting for counterplay
Results swing a lot
tips: When ahead, practice winning by simplifying
Before counterattacking, check that the opponent's threat is really covered
Review your comebacks and find out why you were worse in the first place
AWRO.scene: Even with the knight under attack, the rook gives check first instead of defending

AWRE.tagline: Takes the punches and hits back head-on
AWRE.summary: The Fighter doesn't avoid sharp positions; they meet them head-on. They absorb the opponent's attack with standard defense and pay it back with equal weight. Strong when the opponent overreaches first, but relatively passive about creating their own chances to lead.
traits: Parries threats precisely and hits back right away
weaknesses: Passive about making plans first
Gets lost in quiet positions
Easily pulled into the opponent's pace
tips: Learn plans you can start yourself in quiet positions
Study how to take the initiative when the opponent doesn't overreach
Review the moment you switch from defense to counterattack
AWRE.scene: Two rooks face off head-on along an open file

ASIO.tagline: Waits quietly, then ends the game with a single move
ASIO.summary: The Sniper aims for the decisive shot without overreaching. Normally they set up with safe moves, and the moment a weakness shows up in the enemy camp, they strike precisely with a move others didn't consider. Quiet until the chance comes, but they rarely miss it.
traits: Safe moves most of the time, sharp ones at the critical moment
weaknesses: Games easily end in draws when no chance appears
Hesitates when it's time to shake things up
Few chances against well-prepared opponents
tips: Study how to create chances when none come
Review drawn games for moments you could have won
Solving tactics puzzles regularly sharpens your strength even more
ASIO.scene: A bishop in the corner aims down one diagonal at the queen across the board

ASIE.tagline: Drives the enemy king back with relentless pressure
ASIE.summary: The Commander organizes the attack by moving every piece in order. Without reckless sacrifices they bring pieces into the attack one by one and build pressure until the opponent cracks. Clear plans and few mistakes make for steady wins, but unexpected counterattacks can catch them late.
traits: Takes the initiative and builds pressure slowly
weaknesses: Responding to unexpected counterattacks
Switching plans when the pressure is blocked
So standard it's easy to read
tips: Practice prophylactic moves that remove the opponent's counterplay first
Learn endgame transitions for when the attack is stopped
Now and then, disrupt the opponent's preparation with a surprise
ASIE.scene: Queen, knight and bishop converge on one square to attack the king

ASRO.summary: The Tactician plays moves that look ordinary and safe, but hides traps inside them that are easy to fall into. Rather than attacking directly, they let the opponent move first and slip through the gap with an original tactic. From the other side of the board, it's hard to tell what's dangerous.
traits: Turns the opponent's natural replies against them
weaknesses: Less to do against opponents who avoid the trap
Passive about taking the initiative
Less effective against stronger opponents
tips: Plan your next step for when the trap doesn't work
Remember the same move works differently depending on the opponent's rating
Learn one opening that grabs the initiative early
ASRO.scene: If the queen takes the bait pawn, the knight attacks queen and king at once

ASRE.tagline: Holds firm and makes the opponent pay for every mistake
ASRE.summary: The Prosecutor never overreaches first. They absorb the attack with a solid position, and the moment the opponent slips, they press the point with precise moves all the way. They win cleanly with few ups and downs, but against opponents who don't slip, a decisive result can be hard to get.
weaknesses: Hard to win against opponents who don't err
Passive about stirring things up
Defense can crack under time pressure
tips: Practice creating winning chances even in level positions
Prepare pressure plans for when the opponent makes no mistakes
Check your time management: solid defense needs time on the clock
ASRE.scene: The moment the enemy knight comes in, the rook takes it

PWIO.tagline: Creates imbalance on purpose and builds a new kind of game
PWIO.summary: The Inventor dislikes symmetrical, ordinary positions. They twist the pawn structure on purpose and use trades to create imbalances, designing positions only they understand. They make long-term plans and enjoy risk, which makes them one of the hardest types to predict.
traits: Makes plans few others would make
weaknesses: Hard to recover when the plan is wrong
Loses motivation in simple positions
Tactical mistakes creep in
tips: When making a new plan, check tactical safety first
Learning to win simple positions adds another weapon
Review the unbalanced positions you create with an engine
PWIO.scene: Twisting the pawn structure on purpose to create an unbalanced game

PWIE.tagline: Follows the big picture even in complicated positions
PWIE.summary: The Strategist doesn't lose the big plan when things get complicated. Following proven strategic principles, they gain space and create weaknesses, and they don't shy away from sharp positions while keeping the initiative. A type with a good balance between planning and execution.
traits: Goes for both space and the initiative
Makes plans that follow the principles
weaknesses: Can miss exceptions to the principles
Calculation errors in sharp tactical fights
Thrown off by original moves from the opponent
tips: Practice tactical exceptions to the principles with puzzles
Get in the habit of checking one more candidate move in complicated positions
Review games where the opponent left the main line
PWIE.scene: Pushing pawns side by side to gain space on one wing

PWRO.tagline: Finds clever answers in tangled positions
PWRO.summary: The Fixer shines in hard, tangled positions. While absorbing the opponent's plans, they find inventive solutions instead of ordinary moves and turn crises into chances. Great at holding difficult positions, but also prone to making positions difficult themselves.
traits: Finds surprising solutions in hard positions
Absorbs the opponent's plans while watching for a chance
weaknesses: Makes easy wins complicated
Tends to use a lot of time
Passive about taking the initiative first
tips: In easy positions, practice picking the simplest path
Check your time use: harder positions eat the clock
Learn one opening that grabs the initiative first
PWRO.scene: A king in check finds the one escape square

PWRE.tagline: Survives any mess by sticking to the principles
PWRE.summary: The Survivor holds on by sticking to principles even in messy, uncomfortable positions. When the opponent stirs things up, they stay calm, survive with standard defense and structure management, and take their chance when the opponent tires. Hard to beat, but can be passive about forcing a result.
traits: Holds on until the opponent tires
weaknesses: Passive about forcing a result
Passive positions drag on
Misses sharp counterattacking chances
tips: Look for chances to counterattack even while defending
Decide the game's character first with an opening that takes the initiative
Compare games you saved by defending with ones you lost that way
PWRE.scene: Pieces block attacks coming from three directions

PSIO.tagline: Polishes the position with quiet moves others overlook
PSIO.summary: The Craftsman polishes the position with quiet but precise moves rather than flashy ones. They find small improvements others walk past and stack them up, steering the game their own way. The moves look ordinary, but each one carries an intention.
traits: Lots of quiet but strong moves
weaknesses: Can lose ground in sharp tactical positions
Reacts late to direct attacks
Too cautious at decisive moments
tips: Make a habit of checking the opponent's direct threats first
Practice the decisive moves that turn advantages into wins
Tactics puzzles bring out your strengths by sharpening calculation
PSIO.scene: A knight maneuvers twice to reach a strong square supported by pawns

PSIE.tagline: Slowly squeezes until the opponent runs out of options
PSIE.summary: The Manager plays as if managing the whole board. Holding the initiative, they shrink the range of the opponent's pieces one by one until there is nothing reasonable left to play. They win while taking almost no risk, make few mistakes, and rarely let an advantage slip.
weaknesses: Uncomfortable in wild positions
Slow to commit when a comeback is needed
Loses tempo when the opponent stirs things up
tips: Learn at least one way to shake things up when worse
Prepare answers to sharp openings
Review the difference between squeezing moves and hasty ones
PSIE.scene: A rook seals off the fourth rank and traps the enemy king

PSRO.tagline: Reads the opponent's plan first and answers from an unexpected angle
PSRO.summary: The Thinker first asks what the opponent wants to do. They play prophylactic moves that stop the plan in advance, and find answers in places others don't look. They can look passive, but they are a deep type who leaves the opponent without a plan and off balance.
traits: Stops the opponent's plans in advance
weaknesses: Tends to use a lot of time
Few attempts to win first
Can miss simple tactics
tips: Practice the timing of turning a plan into action
Check your time management
Practice moving on to your own plan after stopping the opponent's
PSRO.scene: A bishop guards the square the enemy knight is aiming for, in advance

PSRE.tagline: Wears the opponent down with a defense that never breaks
PSRE.summary: The Goalkeeper plays chess that, above all, doesn't lose. A solid structure and precise defense stop the opponent's attacks one by one, and when the opponent tires and overreaches, they quietly collect the advantage. The hardest type to break down, though sometimes you have to move first to win.
traits: Waits for the opponent to overreach
weaknesses: Draws pile up
Passive about forcing a result
Passive positions drag on
tips: Practice creating winning chances in safe positions
Compare results when you keep the tension instead of simplifying
Polishing endgame technique lets you win positions you used to only hold
PSRE.scene: A pawn wall in front of the king stops the queen and bishop
